planting.note: Set out plugs or bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun on well-drained, raised beds; Galletta is a North Carolina State University day-neutral release bred for good flavor and consistent production through the warm Southeastern growing season.

directions: Plant on raised, plastic-mulched beds in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and pinch off the first several weeks of flowers on spring-set plants to build a stronger root system before letting the crop set. Galletta is a day-neutral strawberry from the North Carolina State University breeding program, selected to keep flowering and fruiting through summer heat rather than pausing like traditional June-bearers, which gives a longer, more spread-out harvest from spring through fall in the Southeast. Berries are firm, glossy, and well flavored, holding up better to summer warmth than many older day-neutral varieties bred for cooler California conditions. Keep plants consistently watered through hot spells, since day-neutral types are actively fruiting during the stress of summer, and refresh the planting every year or two as vigor declines.

common_name: Portola Strawberry (Vigorous UC Davis Day-Neutral Strawberry)

planting.note: Set out plugs or bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun; Portola is a University of California Davis day-neutral release bred for early, heavy production and holds up well as either a spring or fall planting in mild-winter climates.

directions: Plant on raised, well-drained beds in full sun and feed regularly through the season, since Portola's heavy, near-continuous fruit set draws down soil fertility faster than a typical June-bearer. Released by the University of California, Davis breeding program, Portola is a day-neutral cultivar known for beginning to fruit earlier after planting and producing a notably large early crop compared to older day-neutral varieties, with good-sized, attractive, well-flavored berries throughout the season. It has become a widely grown commercial variety in California for its vigor and productivity, and it performs well for home gardeners willing to keep up with its water and fertility demands. In mild-winter regions it can be planted in fall for a strong spring crop or in spring for summer-into-fall production; renew plantings every one to two years as yields taper off.
sources: University of California Davis Strawberry Breeding Program

common_name: Xie Shan Satsuma (Cold-Hardy Chinese Satsuma Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring after frost danger has passed; Xie Shan is a Chinese satsuma selection popular among cold-hardy citrus growers for its heavy, early production of small, sweet, seedless fruit on a compact tree.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and protect young trees with frost cloth for their first several winters until they gain size and cold hardiness. Xie Shan is a satsuma mandarin selection out of China favored by cold-hardy citrus enthusiasts and Gulf South growers for beginning to bear at a young age and setting unusually heavy crops of small to medium, easy-peel, seedless, sweet fruit that ripen early in the fall citrus season. The compact, naturally dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be given winter protection in the coldest zone 8 locations. As with other satsumas, fruit quality and cold tolerance improve once the tree is well established, so give young trees consistent water and a balanced citrus fertilizer through their first few growing seasons.

common_name: Louisiana Sweet Satsuma (Gulf South Cold-Hardy Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring after frost danger has passed; Louisiana Sweet is a satsuma selection promoted for Gulf Coast dooryard growing for its reliable sweetness and cold tolerance close to that of Owari.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and give young trees frost cloth protection on the coldest nights until they are several years established. Louisiana Sweet is a satsuma mandarin selection grown and promoted along the Gulf Coast for combining good cold hardiness with consistently sweet, low-acid flavor even in years when cooler, cloudier falls can leave other citrus tart. Fruit is medium-sized, nearly seedless, and easy to peel, ripening in the standard satsuma window from October into December ahead of most other citrus. As with all satsumas, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization late in the season, which delays the hardening off trees need to withstand winter cold, and mulch well to protect the root zone.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Monterrey is a Kieffer-type hybrid pear bred for fire blight resistance and reliable production in the hot, humid conditions of Texas and the Gulf South.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator such as Orient or Hood, since Monterrey sets fruit best with a second variety nearby. Like other Kieffer-type hybrid pears bred for the South, Monterrey combines strong resistance to fire blight, the disease that devastates many European dessert pears in the humid Gulf region, with a low chilling requirement that suits mild zone 8-9 winters. Fruit is firm, gritty-textured, and best used cooked, canned, or in preserves rather than eaten fresh off the tree, and it keeps well after harvest, softening gradually in storage. The vigorous, disease-resistant tree needs little spraying compared to European dessert pears, making it a practical low-maintenance choice for home orchards in hot, humid climates.
